Child-benefit cash needs a payment calendar: a July change and a year-end surplus do not fund an earlier bill

Use the official 2026 CCB schedule beside independently entered half-year receipt amounts, then trace first-of-month bills, dedicated funding and a hypothetical receipt delay.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a fixed 2026 benefit-and-expense cash calendar

Extra starting cash required before every modeled bill$450
Dedicated budget balance at 31 December 2026$900

Fixed 2026 educational calendar with independently entered recurring monthly benefit receipts. CRA’s published schedule and base-tax-year mapping are reference facts, not eligibility or amount calculations. Other household cash is assigned on each month’s first day, then the selected child bill is paid; a benefit arriving that same day is credited afterward. The calendar-day lag is an authored stress after each scheduled date, not a forecast of CRA or bank delays. Receipt amounts stay constant within each half-year as a simplifying assumption. Actual entitlements, reassessments, custody or age changes, combined provincial amounts, stopped payments and low-entitlement lump sums are outside this model. Use actual confirmed payment information; inputs do not certify a monthly entitlement. No interest, borrowing or costs outside this dedicated budget are included. Year-end metrics stop on 31 December; the path continues only to collect any delayed 2026 receipts, with no new 2027 costs or resources added.

On this page

  1. Keep the benefit period separate from the calendar year
  2. Enter known receipts rather than inferring an entitlement

The central idea

Confirm the benefit amount and payment pattern independently. A benefit assigned to a later date can support the annual budget while leaving an earlier bill unfunded.

01

Keep the benefit period separate from the calendar year

The CRA’s CCB payment page, updated 22 October 2026 and reviewed here on 25 October, provides twelve scheduled 2026 dates. Its mapping uses the 2024 tax year for January–June payments and the 2025 tax year for July–December payments.

A calendar-year budget can therefore contain portions of two benefit periods. The CRA amount guide explains the annual July recalculation using prior-year adjusted family net income. This is a reference-year relationship, not a calculation of the amount an individual family will receive.

The model takes two independently entered monthly receipt amounts. It does not calculate eligibility, adjusted family net income, child-age effects, custody arrangements or combined provincial benefits. An actual family’s notice and expected payment details must establish the receipt amounts and pattern before they belong in a working cash plan.

02

Enter known receipts rather than inferring an entitlement

The authored default assigns CAD 450 to each scheduled January–June receipt and CAD 600 to each scheduled July–December receipt. Those six-month amounts total CAD 6,300 across the 2026 schedule. They are hypothetical inputs, not published maximum CCB amounts.

Each half-year remains constant solely to make the calendar readable. A reassessment, changed family circumstances, stopped payment or other adjustment may require a more detailed schedule. Entering zero does not decide whether a benefit is payable; it simply removes that assumed receipt from the arithmetic.

Use the monthly model only where a recurring monthly pattern has been independently established. CRA also describes a lump-sum arrangement for low annual entitlements. The calculator does not create that arrangement or transform a small entered amount into a monthly entitlement. No future-year payment schedule is inferred from the 2026 dates.

03

Place the bill before the benefit when that matches the budget

The dedicated budget begins with no opening cash. On every month’s first day, the household assigns CAD 150 from its other resources and then pays a selected CAD 600 child-related bill. The month initially reaches negative CAD 450.

Under the default timing, the first CAD 450 benefit receipt later returns January’s balance to zero. The same pattern repeats through June. A later receipt does not retroactively provide the cash needed on the first day, so the required extra opening reserve is CAD 450.

From July, the selected CAD 600 receipt exceeds that month’s CAD 450 gap by CAD 150. The dedicated balance gradually improves. Other household funding is an allocation from resources outside this sub-budget; it is not a newly created source of total household wealth. Confirm that the allocation is affordable alongside the rest of the family’s commitments.

04

Reconcile the annual surplus separately from the interim reserve

Twelve assignments of CAD 150 provide CAD 1,800. Add CAD 6,300 of benefit receipts and subtract twelve CAD 600 bills, or CAD 7,200. The calendar-year reconciliation leaves CAD 900.

That positive ending amount coexists with the earlier CAD 450 funding requirement. The opening reserve shifts the cash path upward; it does not change the benefit entitlement or make the selected expense cheaper. Looking only at the annual surplus would miss the need to fund the first bill before its later receipt.

The waterfall stops on 31 December. It includes only receipts that the selected timing places inside 2026. A delayed receipt arriving after that date belongs in the later collection segment, not in the year-end cash balance. The chart data retains the full dates of each funding assignment, bill and receipt.

05

Test a receipt delay without presenting it as a forecast

The lag control adds a hypothetical number of calendar days after every scheduled date. It does not alter CRA’s published schedule, predict a processing delay or guarantee that a bank balance will be available at a particular time.

With a 14-day lag in the default, all selected receipts still arrive during 2026, and the final balance remains CAD 900. The required opening cash increases to CAD 900 because another first-of-month bill can arrive before the delayed receipt.

At 35 days, the selected December receipt moves to 15 January 2027. The 2026 balance becomes CAD 300; the later CAD 600 receipt brings the collection-only endpoint to CAD 900. No 2027 bill or additional household funding is modeled during that runoff segment, so it is not a complete forecast of the following year.

06

Keep the dedicated reserve connected to actual family cash flow

The matrix changes the opening reserve and other monthly household funding while retaining the benefit inputs, selected bill and lag. Each cell reports extra starting cash required to keep every modeled bill funded. It does not report extra benefits, a tax saving or a probability of a shortfall.

For implementation, confirm the actual expected receipts, list the relevant bills and place both on a calendar with other income. Keep costs entered here separate from costs already included elsewhere, and count each reserved dollar once. A bill already paid from another budget should not be deducted again without transferring its funding too.

Review the plan after a confirmed payment or cost change. This is a fixed-year cash illustration, not an application tool or an entitlement calculator. Its purpose is to show when supported resources arrive, how much cash is needed beforehand and why the timing question remains important even when the annual total looks comfortable.
